name: Tomas Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to employers, unions, government or AI firms. Your answers are confidential. Tomas, what is an ordinary day on the lines?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: We take the permit, check the van load and drive to a broken span or a new connection. I like a sound connection and an apprentice who learns why the test matters. I get tired of drawings that make a difficult lift look like a quick stop, so I keep the tension and torque readings in a pocket book.

say: I would say **sound guy wires** and safe connections still need lineworkers.
I would keep **hand measurements** and a printed permit at the site.
think: I have **never used AI** and expect regular line shifts to continue.
Our **four-month reserve** can cover one delayed callout.
do: Keep paid **line shifts** and teach the apprentice wire tension checks.
Write **torque readings** in the pocket book during the first year.
feel: I feel **settled about wages** while watching family costs.
S0.quote: I do not want a typo travelling farther than the crew.
fieldNote: Tomas trusts **measured wire tension** after a quarry bend fault that looked harmless from the road.
His **four-month savings**, typical pay and some nearby employers support a calm response to minor office automation.

steps.text: Continue paid line repairs and hand-check wire tension with the apprentice

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that a faster report is fine, but the pole still needs a sound guy wire and a safe connection. I learned the work by watching a journeyman, not a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have never used AI, and a little office automation would not make me change jobs. We have about four months of expenses saved, my regular pay covers the mortgage and there are a few other line employers within a drive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the line rota and carry on teaching the apprentice how to check wire tension by hand. In the first year I would keep using the printed permit and the torque readings in my pocket book.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel settled about earning. My partner and I watch the children's costs, but a single delayed callout would not put the mortgage at risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the pocket book tell you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the quarry bend, the wire looked straight from the road but the measured tension was low. I wrote the reading down so the next crew would not trust the photograph.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you let a computer fill in the reading?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It can copy the number after I measure it, but I would keep my written mark. I do not want a typo travelling farther than the crew.

say: I would challenge a **two-person target** for a lift needing three people.
I would ask for **site time** to include isolation and traffic control.
think: I expect **office roles** to shrink while line repairs continue.
A **rushed schedule** could remove paid inspection time.
do: Keep paid **line shifts** and record targets missing safety time.
Bring **signed job sheets** to the supervisor in the first rollout year.
feel: I feel **wary for the crew** without expecting an immediate wage loss.
S1.quote: The person on the pole sees the job the office cannot.
fieldNote: Tomas accepts **cost savings** in principle but rejects schedule targets that omit physical lifting and traffic control.
He prefers **signed job sheets** and a supervisor discussion before asking a union representative to intervene.

steps.text: Continue paid line shifts during scheduling changes
Ask the union representative to join a crew meeting if unsafe targets persist

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the depot that it may buy scheduling software, but it should not tell a two-person crew to do a three-person lift. The person on the pole sees the job the office cannot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The planning and buying desks might lose people first. I expect my own repairs to continue, though a rushed schedule could take away the paid time needed to inspect the quarry bend properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my shifts and write down any target that leaves out isolation or lifting time. In the first rollout year I would bring two completed job sheets to the supervisor and ask for the time allowance to be corrected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel wary for the crew, not in danger of losing my wage tomorrow. I do not mind a company saving money if the actual job remains safe and the pay remains honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which job sheets would you bring?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would bring the quarry bend repair and the school gate pole, where traffic control took longer than the lift. Both have signatures showing the time we were on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask for a union meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would go to the supervisor with the signed sheets first. If the new target stayed in place after that, I would ask the union representative to join a crew meeting.

say: I would separate **2028 planning AI** from line robots around 2031.
I would require a **journeyman check** on early robot connections.
think: At **48**, physical line shifts could shrink when robots arrive.
Our **four-month reserve** cannot carry a long mortgage gap.
do: Keep paid **repairs** in 2029 and check nearby posted line vacancies.
Apply if **crew hours fall** and ask about paid field maintenance training.
feel: I feel **worried about 2031** while expecting wages in 2028.
S2.quote: A set of online lessons after supper would take time from my family without proving I can do the job.
fieldNote: Tomas protects **paid field work** in the three-year gap and looks at nearby employers before making a risky move.
His **apprenticeship preference** requires hands-on paid instruction and a named vacancy, not an unpaid online course.

steps.text: Continue paid line repair shifts through 2029
Apply for a posted nearby line job if his crew hours fall
Take paid hands-on maintenance training if linked to a named vacancy

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues that full AI in 2028 can write plans, but robots able to work the line come around 2031. I would want a human journeyman to check each early robot-made connection.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 45 when the office changes and 48 when robots reach our physical work. Four months of expenses would let us look for another line job, but they would not keep the mortgage paid for long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would call the two nearby utilities to ask whether they post line vacancies and keep my present shifts. In 2029 I would continue repairs, apply for a posted line job if our crew hours fell and ask the company about paid practical training for a field maintenance post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel worried about the 2031 field date, though the wages do not vanish in 2028. My children need a steady home, and I would not tell them the family has to move on the strength of a forecast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would practical training have to offer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want a working maintenance crew, a paid instructor and a named vacancy at the end. A set of online lessons after supper would take time from my family without proving I can do the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the savings for a course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the reserve is for mortgage payments if work stops. If an employer wants me trained for a real opening, the training hours should be paid.

say: I would request **windy field trials** before robots take line jobs.
I would note **2031 planning AI** arrives before hands-on robots around 2034.
think: At **51**, I may still need full wages for the mortgage.
A **report-heavy maintenance job** could shrink under full AI.
do: Keep paid **line shifts** in 2032 and watch a robot field trial.
Apply for **posted substation maintenance** if pay matches and accept funded practical training.
feel: I feel **less pressed** with time to inspect real jobs.
S3.quote: A clean training shed is the easy part of proving a line-repair robot.
fieldNote: Tomas wants **poor-weather evidence** and human checks on final joints before robots receive live work.
He investigates **physical substation maintenance**, knowing full AI could absorb the report-heavy portion.

steps.text: Apply for a posted substation field maintenance role if pay matches
Take the employer-funded practical maintenance course if required

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years is enough to show what a robot can do in wind, not just in a training shed. Full AI comes to planning in 2031, while field robots arrive around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 48 when plans change and 51 when robots can handle lines. Our older child may be leaving school, but I cannot assume the mortgage is gone or that I can retire at 51.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask the neighbouring utility about paid substation field maintenance openings and keep my line rota. In 2032 I would watch a robot field trial on paid time, apply for a posted maintenance role if the wage matched and take its practical course if the employer funded it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel less pressed than in the fast picture. Five years lets me see a real job and a real machine before risking the wage my family uses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask about substation maintenance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask whether the crew physically tests equipment on site or mainly fills in reports. Full AI could do the reports, and I would not trade climbing for a desk that is about to shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you let a robot take a live job after one trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would want several repairs in poor weather and a human check of each final connection. A clean training shed is the easy part of proving a line-repair robot.

say: I would ask for a **yearly line-hour count** as robots develop.
I would distinguish **2036 office AI** from field robots around 2039.
think: At **56**, grown children do not provide a pension or clear the mortgage.
I would consider **field maintenance** if paid line shifts actually fall.
do: Keep paid **line repairs** in 2037 and review annual hours with my partner.
Apply for **posted maintenance work** only if shifts shrink and pay matches.
feel: I feel **steady now** and cautious about later robot repairs.
S4.quote: I can stay with the trade while learning from actual trials, without setting a retirement date from a machine timetable.
fieldNote: Tomas expects **continued paid line work** over the next years and keeps the existing savings reserve intact.
He links any **field transfer** to observed lost shifts and comparable pay rather than a distant robot timetable.

steps.text: Continue paid line repair shifts through 2037
Apply for a posted field maintenance job if line shifts fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that a decade lets us keep teaching safe work while the company tests machines. Full AI changes the office around 2036, and robots doing line repairs come around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 when the office changes and 56 when robots reach the field. The children may be adults then, but I cannot treat that as a pension or assume the mortgage is finished.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep the paid repair rota and ask for a yearly count of line hours. In 2037 I would keep working, review the count with my partner and apply for a posted field maintenance role only if my shifts began falling and the pay was similar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel steady for the years in front of me. I can stay with the trade while learning from actual trials, without setting a retirement date from a machine timetable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay off the mortgage early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We have four months of expenses saved and keep making the agreed payments. I would not empty the reserve because a possible robot date is around thirteen years away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell an apprentice in 2037?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell a new apprentice to learn the line craft and keep records of every safety ticket. I would also say a trade is worth practising even when the equipment changes.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Which picture worries you most, and what would actually help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because robots could reach physical line work around 2031 while the children still need a home paid for. Real trials in poor weather, a posted nearby field job and employer-paid practical training would give us choices.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who checks the final joint when a machine makes it. A family loses power when a repair fails, regardless of who signed the work order.

headlineQuote: A family loses power when a repair fails, regardless of who signed the work order.
portrait: Tomas is a **43-year-old lineworker** with an apprenticeship, a partner, two school-age children and a mortgage.
He has **never used AI** and trusts hand measurements, printed permits and practical instruction.
His **four-month reserve**, typical pay and some nearby employers give room to seek another field job.
Across the scenarios he protects **paid line shifts** and considers only posted physical work with comparable pay.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** leaves about three years before robots could take on physical line repairs.
whatWouldHelp: Real **poor-weather trials**, a posted nearby field role and employer-paid practical training would give his family options.
